<reason>CON was the more vivid and aggressive debater, and its pressure question extracted a genuine concession ("Yes, under this rule alone" the dark-patterned sale is lawful). But CON's central claim—that consent creates "a lawful pathway around" a use ban and "certifies" dangerous sales—was logically defective, and PRO exposed it cleanly: the motion prohibits sales without consent and neither repeals nor requires permitting anything else. Under pressure CON retreated to "the motion contains no use ban," which is true but only shows incompleteness, not harm; the "political appetite evaporates" claim was late speculation. PRO's Q2 then forced CON to admit its minimization alternative bans even more sales, letting PRO frame the motion as a floor CON itself wants to exceed. CON's rejoinder that these are "not weaker and stronger versions of one rule" was assertion rather than argument. PRO also parried the abuser-thumb and vulnerability points adequately (imperfect consent isn't universal consent; CON likewise can't detect buyer intent in advance). Two clipped CON turns were an added execution cost. PRO wins a competitive debate on tighter logic and a cleaner decision rule.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's [B4.5]/[B4.8]/[B5.1] sequence: holding CON's proposed prohibitions constant, the consent rule only removes unpermitted sales, and CON's own minimization answer commits it to prohibiting the very transactions the motion restricts—turning CON's alternative into an argument for a stronger version of the motion rather than against it.</best_rebuttal>
